tldr: By leveraging the high-level semantic reasoning of Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models while physically "caging" their motions via low-dimensional MPPI integrated with Signed Distance Fields (SDF) and discrete Exponential Barrier Functions (dEBF), this work achieves zero-collision natural language navigation on humanoid and quadrupedal robots.
hero_caption: Overall framework of the proposed method. The top semantic grounding layer (VLA/VLM and object detection) proposes navigation goals from language instructions, while the bottom physical grounding layer (LiDAR/odometry, local SDF, and dEBF-MPPI control) strictly guarantees geometric collision avoidance and converts them into executable velocity commands.
overview:
With the recent advancement of Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, directing robots autonomously using natural language—such as "go to the trash can over there"—is becoming a reality. However, while existing end-to-end VLA models excel at commonsense semantic reasoning, they fail to consider the robot's physical body footprint, metric distance to surrounding obstacles, and explicit safety constraints. Consequently, deploying them directly in the real world risks colliding with walls or producing kinematically infeasible trajectories.

Rather than abandoning the powerful semantic reasoning of VLAs, the authors propose a "caging" architecture that treats VLA outputs as mere "proposals" and encloses them within a control-theoretic safety net. Specifically, coarse movement commands generated by the high-level VLA are projected into executable, safe target poses using an online-built Signed Distance Field (SDF: a map representing the shortest distance to obstacle surfaces). In the lower layer, a low-dimensional Bézier-parameterized Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) planner incorporating discrete-time Exponential Barrier Functions (dEBF) runs to guarantee mathematically provable collision avoidance.

The system was evaluated across diverse indoor and outdoor environments using real hardware: the Unitree G1 humanoid and the Ghost Robotics Vision 60 quadruped. In long-horizon tasks within a 12m × 12m environment, baseline navigation without caging collided in all 60 trials, whereas applying the proposed method achieved a 0% collision rate. It is a practical framework that safely tames the unconstrained proposals of powerful AI models within a cage of geometry and control theory.
contributions: Construction of a two-layer caging architecture that treats VLA/VLM semantic reasoning as high-level proposals, decoupling safety assurance from geometric feasibility

Proposal of a Bézier-parameterized MPPI planner that queries only local SDF values without requiring gradient computations, ensuring strict collision avoidance via discrete Exponential Barrier Functions (dEBF)
Implementation of an open-vocabulary object-centric grounding module (Grounding-DINO and SAM2) that achieves precise terminal positioning toward target objects (mean error of 0.29m)

Proof of effectiveness and platform-agnostic capability through comprehensive real-world experiments on both humanoid (Unitree G1) and quadruped (Vision 60) platforms using multiple commercial and open-source VLMs

sections.heading: How do we balance VLA intelligence with real-world safety?
sections.summary: Natural language navigation is essential for legged robots to collaborate with humans, but existing VLAs cannot account for physical collision constraints. This work proposes "caging," a novel framework that takes VLA reasoning as high-level proposals and mathematically guarantees safety in a lower physical-grounding layer.
sections.details:
When deploying humanoid and quadrupedal robots in human environments, the most fundamental capability is safely navigating to designated locations. Traditionally, this required pre-built behavior trees or skilled operators setting target coordinates. However, recent advances in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and VLAs are making flexible vision-language navigation (VLN) possible using natural language.

Yet, a serious challenge remains. Pretrained VLA models excel at visual and semantic commonsense reasoning—such as deciding which room to enter—but they overlook robot kinematics, local obstacle layouts, and strict closed-loop safety constraints. As a result, end-to-end action generation readily outputs physically infeasible paths or commands that crash directly into obstacles.

To address this, the authors do not feed VLA outputs straight to the robot's locomotion controller; instead, they treat them strictly as "high-level proposals." A safety layer is inserted to verify and refine these proposed trajectories based on online geometric perception and control barrier functions. Termed "caging," this approach aims to mathematically guarantee collision avoidance while fully retaining the flexibility of pretrained models.

sections.heading: Decoupling semantic understanding from geometric safety: A critical departure from prior work
sections.summary: Unlike prior safety-aware VLAs that relied on model retraining or focused strictly on manipulation, this approach cages the system via an external safety layer without modifying the VLA itself. Furthermore, combining MPPI with barrier functions eliminates distance field gradient calculations, dramatically reducing computational load.
sections.details:
Recent legged VLN research includes works like QUAR-VLA for quadrupeds and NaVILA for legged systems. While they propose strong semantic behaviors, they lack safety mechanisms that strictly consider the robot's physical footprint and surrounding obstacle geometry. Methods like SafeVLA enhance safety through constrained training, and AEGIS corrects manipulation outputs using Control Barrier Functions (CBFs). However, these require retraining the models or cannot be easily applied to legged robot navigation.

The cleverness of this work lies in leaving the high-level semantic model completely untouched. The front-end, which infers coarse targets from language instructions and camera images, is completely separated from the back-end, which steers the robot safely around obstacles. Consequently, whether switching the VLM/VLA from GPT-4 to Claude or Gemini, or swapping the robot from a humanoid to a quadruped, the safety layer functions seamlessly without modification.

Moreover, when incorporating barrier functions into sampling-based model predictive control (MPPI), most prior studies required computing map gradients or solving complex quadratic programs (QPs). In contrast, this method directly uses online-updated local SDF values (raw distance information) to evaluate sampled trajectories. This enables exceptionally fast and stable execution, even with non-differentiable costs and non-smooth maps.

sections.heading: A two-layer system architecture dividing semantic and physical duties
sections.summary: The overall system consists of two layers: the "semantic grounding layer" and the "physical grounding layer." Abstracting robot dynamics into a planar velocity model and representing the environment via a local SDF provides a unified safety control interface across different robot platforms.
sections.details:
The goal of this system is to generate real-time velocity command sequences $\{\mathbf{u}_k\}$ that guide the robot toward target regions or objects from high-level natural language instructions and onboard sensor inputs (cameras, LiDAR, IMU) without violating collision constraints.

### III-A Robot and Environment Modeling
The robot pose is represented on a 2D plane as $\mathbf{x} = [p_x, p_y, \psi]^\top$ (position and yaw), with control inputs being body-frame linear and angular velocities $\mathbf{u}_k = [v_x, v_y, \omega]^\top$ under a discrete-time constant-velocity model. This planar twist model allows bipedal and quadrupedal gaits—two completely different locomotion mechanisms—to be treated uniformly through the same kinematic interface.
The surrounding obstacle environment is represented as a 2D Signed Distance Field (SDF) $\phi(\mathbf{p})$. Here, $\phi(\mathbf{p}) > 0$ denotes navigable free space, $\phi(\mathbf{p}) = 0$ marks obstacle surfaces, and $\phi(\mathbf{p}) < 0$ indicates obstacle interiors, enabling instantaneous distance queries to the nearest obstacle from any coordinate.

### III-B Proposed Caging Framework
The system is split into two primary layers:
- **Semantic Grounding Layer**: The VLM/VLA generates discrete high-level actions (e.g., "turn right 15 degrees," "move forward 50 cm") from instructions and images. The Kinematic Goal Projector cross-references these with the SDF, transforming them into executable 2D goal poses $\mathbf{x}^{\mathrm{goal}}$ that are free of surrounding obstacles.
- **Physical Grounding Layer**: Accurate state estimation is provided by LiDAR odometry (FastLIVO2) for the humanoid, and an invariant EKF fusing leg kinematics and IMU for the quadruped. A low-dimensional MPPI planner with SDF and dEBF constraints then outputs safe velocity commands toward the goal pose in real time. A global Jump Point Search (JPS) path planner can also be combined when necessary.

sections.heading: Translating language instructions into safe geometric goals and terminal approaches
sections.summary: Discrete actions from the VLA are projected onto safe target coordinates at least 0.3m away from obstacles using the SDF. Right before task completion, open-vocabulary models (Grounding-DINO + SAM2) are activated to perform precise terminal docking to the specified object.
sections.details:
In the upper semantic grounding layer, two modules ensure that VLA outputs are grounded into physically viable targets rather than directly driving actuators.

### Kinematic Goal Projector
Treating predicted VLA actions like "move forward 75 cm" or "turn left 30 degrees" directly as targets can result in goal points located inside walls. This module queries the local SDF to check whether candidate position $\mathbf{p}$ satisfies a safety clearance threshold $d_{\mathrm{clear}} = 0.3\,\mathrm{m}$. If the position collides with an obstacle, candidate poses are sampled within a neighborhood radius, and an optimal alternative target pose is selected using a cost function that balances proximity to the original goal, alignment with the robot's heading, and obstacle clearance. This guarantees that the low-level planner is always fed safe targets.

### Open-Vocabulary Object-Centric Grounding Module
To precisely execute instructions such as "stop in front of the trash can" during the final phase of navigation, Grounding-DINO (open-vocabulary detector) is paired with SAM2 (high-precision segmentation). Bounding boxes and masks matching text prompts are extracted from camera images, and 3D global coordinates are computed using LiDAR point clouds and camera intrinsics. To eliminate false detections, only targets within a distance of $0.5\,\mathrm{m} \le d \le 3.0\,\mathrm{m}$ from the robot are accepted, and the robot halts neatly once the distance drops below $d_{\mathrm{stop}} = 0.50\,\mathrm{m}$.

sections.heading: Strict safety guarantees via low-dimensional MPPI and discrete Exponential Barrier Functions (dEBF)
sections.summary: Trajectory parameterization via Bézier curves enables low-dimensional, smooth exploration, while discrete Exponential Barrier Functions (dEBF) constrain approach speeds toward obstacles. A hard candidate filtering step and a 1-step safety backup control guarantee zero collisions (forward invariance) under stated assumptions.
sections.details:
The physical grounding layer forms the core "protective cage" that turns semantic targets $\mathbf{x}^{\mathrm{goal}}$ into safe physical motions. This method embeds geometric barrier function constraints directly into MPPI, a sampling-based stochastic optimal control framework.

### V-A & V-B Low-Dimensional Bézier MPPI and Cost Design
Standard MPPI samples control inputs at every time step across the prediction horizon, resulting in high dimensionality and often jerky robot commands. This work parameterizes the control input sequence using a degree-$d$ Bézier curve (control points $P_j$). This compresses the search dimension drastically while restricting sampled trajectories to structurally smooth velocity profiles. Each rollout is evaluated using a weighted sum of goal-reaching costs (following travel direction when far, aligning smoothly with terminal yaw when close) and velocity violation penalties.

### V-C SDF-Based dEBF Constraints and Safety Proofs
Safety is enforced using discrete-time Exponential Barrier Functions (dEBF). Defining the safe set as $h(\mathbf{x}) \ge 0$, the dEBF condition is expressed as:
$$h(\mathbf{x}_{k+1}) - h(\mathbf{x}_k) \ge - (1 - \gamma) h(\mathbf{x}_k)$$
where $\gamma \in [0, 1)$ is a decay parameter determining conservatism. As the robot nears obstacles ($h(\mathbf{x}) \to 0$), permissible approach velocity shrinks to zero, naturally decelerating the robot before impact. The robot geometry is approximated using multiple rigid bounding spheres (Figure F2), querying clearances directly from the SDF at each sphere center to evaluate barrier values.

Algorithmically, MPPI rollouts violating dEBF conditions incur penalty costs to bias sampling toward safe trajectories; ultimately, the lowest-cost rollout that fully satisfies all barrier conditions is executed. In the rare event that all candidates violate constraints, a "1-step safety backup control" such as zero velocity (stopping) is applied. Through mathematical induction, the safe set is proven to be forward invariant (once safe, always safe) under Theorem 1.

captions.F2: Geometric robot safety models. (a) Vision 60 (quadruped) and (b) Unitree G1 (humanoid). The entire body is covered with multiple spheres, enabling fast, accurate collision checks with only a few SDF clearance queries at the center points.

sections.heading: Real-world humanoid and quadruped experiments prove dramatic collision reduction
sections.summary: Evaluations in simulation and on real hardware (G1 and Vision 60) demonstrated that dEBF reliably slows down and avoids collisions in narrow passages and sudden obstacle incursions compared to standard MPPI. Notably, in 12m × 12m long-horizon tasks, caging achieved a 0% collision rate, compared to 100% without caging.
sections.details:
Comprehensive evaluations across simulation (Gazebo) and real robots (humanoid Unitree G1, quadruped Vision 60) assessed dEBF behavior, static and dynamic obstacle avoidance, and long-horizon navigation safety. MPPI parameters were set to 200 samples, 10 iterations, a 2.5-second prediction horizon (50 steps), and $\gamma = 0.95$.

### VI-B Simulation Analysis of dEBF Characteristics
As shown in Figure F3, larger decay parameters $\gamma$ maintain greater clearance from obstacles. While conventional penalty-based MPPI tends to maintain high speed into narrow gaps, incorporating dEBF ensures smooth deceleration as obstacles approach, allowing safe passage.

### VI-C Control Ablation in G1 Arena
Experiments in a 4m × 4m environment evaluated four LLM/VLM front-ends (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, NaVILA). With static obstacles and no global JPS planner, standard MPPI suffered an 80% collision rate (CR), whereas enabling dEBF dropped collisions to 0%. When obstacles were abruptly placed in the robot's path during motion (with JPS enabled), standard MPPI collided 100% of the time during replanning latency, but dEBF maintained a 0% collision rate, boosting end-to-end task success from 0% to 70%.

### VI-D & VI-E Large-Scale Environments and Cross-Platform Validation
In 15 long-distance navigation tasks (120 trials total) within a 12m × 12m area, turning off the caging mechanism resulted in collisions in all 60 trials (100% CR). Conversely, with the proposed caging active across 60 trials, collisions were completely eliminated (0% CR) across all four front-ends. Furthermore, indoor and outdoor experiments on the Vision 60 quadruped reduced collision rates in complex tasks from 0.91 to 0.08, confirming unified safety protection across distinct platforms.

### VI-F Object-Centric Grounding Approach Accuracy
On the Vision 60, enabling Grounding-DINO + SAM2 terminal grounding improved mean stopping position error (Navigation Error) toward target objects from 1.50m down to 0.29m, confirming precise positioning within reachable interaction range.

(b) Velocity profiles in narrow corridors (penalty-based MPPI charges ahead, whereas dEBF decelerates naturally). (c) Smooth terminal approach behavior toward target objects.

sections.heading: Conclusions and future outlook: From locomotion to whole-body manipulation
sections.summary: This work establishes a modular architecture cleanly separating VLA semantic reasoning from control-theoretic safety assurance. Future directions include addressing mapping and odometry uncertainties, handling dynamic obstacles theoretically, and extending the framework to whole-body tasks like grasping.
sections.details:
This study proposed and validated "caging"—a practical framework providing physical safety indispensable for real-world legged robotics while preserving the rich semantic capabilities of pretrained VLM/VLA models. By integrating local SDFs and dEBF into Bézier MPPI, the framework achieves theoretical collision avoidance with low computational overhead, proven effective on both humanoid and quadrupedal robots.

The authors highlight three key future directions. First, explicitly incorporating real-world sensing uncertainties into safety analyses, including LiDAR blind spots, mapping delays, and odometry drift. Second, extending theoretical guarantees to dynamic environments with moving obstacles. Third, expanding caging beyond locomotion to whole-body coordinated manipulation skills, such as humanoid grasping and object handover. Combining these capabilities with multimodal memory holds promise for realizing truly general-purpose, safe personal assistant robots.

takeaways: Instead of "training safety into the VLA," "caging it with an external control layer (SDF + dEBF + MPPI)" is key to achieving both real-world safety and model interchangeability

Because discrete Exponential Barrier Functions (dEBF) constrain approach velocities alongside distances, they effectively prevent high-speed entries into narrow passages and subsequent collisions common in penalty-based MPPI
Compressing the MPPI search space via Bézier curve parameterization and querying only raw local SDF values enables a gradient-free, fast, and smooth real-time safety control loop
Global coarse guidance (JPS) and local real-time protection (dEBF) are complementary, significantly boosting robustness during dynamic map updates
limitations: Theoretical safety guarantees rely on the assumption that obstacles are correctly perceived in the SDF; obstacles missing from point clouds (e.g., LiDAR blind spots, thin wires, sharp table edges) cannot be avoided
The 2D planar constant-velocity twist model does not account for slippage during aggressive acceleration/deceleration, sudden tracking delays, or rapid odometry drift
While the caging layer prevents physical collisions, it cannot rescue task failures caused by the high-level VLA proposing semantically incorrect destinations (e.g., wrong rooms or unreachable goals)
